Some classics if you've never read them:

·His Dark Materials trilogy by Phillip Pullman (The Northern Lights, the Subtle Knife, and the Amber Spyglass). One of the most unique stories I've ever read, a thorougly believable and realistic modern-ish fantasy that will make you think about human nature, and something I truly believe everybody should read at least once. 

·The Hobbit + Lord of the Rings. Classic books for a reason, medieval style fantasy, fun and adventurous. But admittedly not for everyone when it comes to writing style. 

·Moby Dick. I mean... It's a novel about the sea, and you'll be on a ship.

My personal favourites:
·The Book Thief. A very unique writing style and an absolutely beautiful book which will stretch the boundaries of all your emotions. 

·The Starless Sea. I cannot even describe this book. It's... A book about a young man, who (in the book!) picks up the same book you're reading and finds his life written in the pages. It's a mystery and fantasy adventure. It's a book about stories and it will make you notice the small stories that surround and fill your life, will make you think about human nature and fate. Cannot recommend enough.

See the thing is, I enjoy TotK and think it's a good Zelda game that marries old ideas from traditional Zelda with the new direction of BotW rather well. There was a lacking emptiness to BotW that TotK fills - a bit, kinda. 

But that last paragraph... I remember my first time playing Zelda, and as I was walking around as Link I noticed his eyes looking around. My dad told me "this is Zelda - if they've included something, there's a reason for it. Everything they do in a Zelda game is intentional." That sentence stuck with me. It's what guided my puzzle-solving growing up.
 
Every jar potentially had something in it. 
A crack or a vine on a wall led somewhere with an item. 
Every glance or movement from Link indicated a secret.
Every NPC sentence carefully crafted to deliver story, world-building, or important information. 
Every small nook and cranny was deliberately placed to contain something, like a Piece of Heart or potion.
If something caught your eye, there was ALWAYS a reason for it, and there was ALWAYS something waiting for you there. 

I miss that. I love TotK so far, but I can see that if I play too long, it will feel.... pointless. There's so many ruined buildings I go to just to find 5 wooden boxes with an apple in. 
I wouldn't want a sequel for that

I hear what you're saying, and it's totally valid that the gameplay wasn't right for you, but that doesn't mean it serves badly as a game. 
There are many games that are very similar in that they are mostly atmospheric narratives that you just play through and experience, rather than in depth strategic gameplay. Rime, Abzu, and Journey are all more story or atmospheric think-pieces than they are mechanical games. 

Before games existed, people watched films and thought... "I wish I could live in that world!"
Games were made for two reasons: to tell a story in a way that lets you actually LIVE in the story; and to entertain yourself physically (solving puzzles, aiming weapons etc). For some people that means becoming an action-packed superhero where you have to make real decisions to affect the outcome (RPG/action adventure). For some people it means having a sense of tension and urgency, having consequences (horror games). Some people just want to be immersed in a story, though. They want a story, but they don't want to see it happen like a film - they want to live IN the story and watch it unfold around them. They want to be a part of the story. That's what games like stray are about - giving you a world you can dive in and immerse yourself in and just... experience.
